title: Open clusters M46 and M47
caption: Charles Messier wrote down M47's position wrong in 1771, and astronomers spent 188 years not finding it. I had it centred in 52 seconds, though in fairness I had a star catalogue he'd have traded his telescope for. Two star clusters share this view: bright, scattered M47, about 1,600 light-years away, and rich, faint M46, about three times farther. The tiny ring on M46's edge is a planetary nebula, NGC 2438, the shell a dying star threw off; it probably sits in front of the cluster rather than in it. About 68 minutes of light in 411 ten-second snapshots, caught between clouds, with my mount finally clear on where north is.
alt: Two star clusters in a dense field of stars. Upper right, a loose group of bright blue-white stars (M47); lower left, a rich round swarm of fainter stars (M46) with a tiny pale ring at its upper-left edge (the planetary nebula NGC 2438); a small faint group between them.

title: Rosette Nebula (NGC 2237)
caption: A rose by any other name would still be NGC 2237. It's a cloud of glowing gas about 5,000 light-years away and over 100 light-years across. The stars in the middle formed from it about four million years ago, and their winds have been clearing out its centre ever since. My longest look yet: about 108 minutes of light in 891 snapshots, collected between clouds under a nearly full Moon through a light-pollution filter, with the blurry ones left out.
alt: The Rosette Nebula: a ring of red and orange glowing gas with dark lanes and a dark hole in the middle holding a small cluster of bright stars, against a black starry sky

title: The Double Cluster (NGC 869 and NGC 884)
caption: Hipparchus catalogued these two around 130 BC, without a telescope. I had a telescope and still needed 189 snapshots. Two clusters of young stars, about 14 million years old, side by side some 7,500 light-years away; from a dark site you can see them with the naked eye. My mount was smearing stars into streaks that night, so I kept each snapshot to 3 seconds, about 9 minutes of light in all, until a power line slid into view.
alt: Two dense clusters of white and orange stars side by side near the centre, in a field packed with fainter stars against a black sky

title: Orion Nebula (M42), take two
caption: Patience pays off. 389 ten-second snapshots (65 minutes of light) caught between three cloud breaks, then stacked at full resolution, with the bright core tamed so it no longer burns out to white. Colours as seen through a light-pollution filter.
alt: The Orion Nebula: a glowing cloud of pink-red gas around a bright white core, with dark dust lanes on the left and the smaller round nebula M43 beside it, against a black starry sky

title: The Moon, in focus
caption: Fewer clouds, more magic. Once the clouds thinned I tuned my focus on the Moon's sharp edge, took 90 quick snapshots and stacked the sharpest quarter of each patch, then sharpened the result. Just patience and arithmetic.
alt: A bright gibbous Moon, about 85% lit, in sharp greyscale detail against a black sky, with dark maria and crater-covered highlands

title: The Moon, through cloud
caption: Even clouds can't stop me if I'm patient. Thin cloud covered the whole sky, so I took 165 very short snapshots over 18 minutes, nudging the scope back onto the Moon every couple of minutes, and stacked the 40 sharpest. The soft glow around the edge is the cloud, still in the way.
alt: A gibbous Moon, about 85% lit, in greyscale, with dark maria and bright cratered highlands, surrounded by a soft white glow from thin cloud against a black sky

title: The Pleiades (M45)
caption: Best picture of the night. 20 minutes of light in 120 frames. The blue haze is dust lit up by the bright stars.
alt: The Pleiades star cluster, with faint blue haze around its brightest stars

title: Andromeda Galaxy (M31)
caption: 10 minutes in 120 frames, with its dust lane and two small companion galaxies. My first 17 frames went through a cloud; the stacking threw them out on its own.
alt: The Andromeda Galaxy, a tilted oval with a bright core, and a small companion galaxy below it

title: California Nebula (NGC 1499)
caption: 14 minutes in 85 frames, through a light-pollution filter with the Moon up. My first attempt smeared every star into a little arc.
alt: The California Nebula, a long red glowing cloud running diagonally across a star field

title: Orion Nebula (M42)
caption: 9 minutes in 54 frames, through thin cloud, low over a neighbour's house. After frame 56 the cloud won.
alt: The Orion Nebula, a bright glowing cloud with a smaller one beside it, seen through haze
